    Calculation of the doubles: (i) 2 × 35° = 70°; (ii) 2 × 42° = 84°; (iii) 2 × 70° = 140°.
    Finished figure: At B on base BC, two equal arc-steps K to L and L to M are marked along one big arc, and ray BA through M makes the doubled angle with BC.
    Answer: The constructed angles measure (i) 70°, (ii) 84°, (iii) 140°.
  • Q: Q3. Construct angles of the following measures with the help of protractor: (i) 76° (ii) 68° (iii) 98°. Bisect these angles with the help of compasses. Measure each part.
    Ans: Part 1 — with a protractor: Draw each angle with a protractor as in Q1: (i) 76°, (ii) 68°, (iii) 98°. Call a given angle ∠ABC with vertex B.
    Part 2 — bisecting with compasses (same method for each angle):
    Step 1: With B as centre and a suitable radius, draw an arc cutting BA at one point and BC at another point.
    Step 2: With each of these two points as centre in turn, and radius more than half the distance between them, draw two arcs inside the angle cutting each other at a point, say D.
    Step 3: Join B to D. Ray BD is the bisector, so the two parts are equal.
    Measure of each part = given angle ÷ 2:
    (i) 76° ÷ 2 = 38°
    (ii) 68° ÷ 2 = 34°
    (iii) 98° ÷ 2 = 49°
    Finished figure: Each angle is split by an inside ray from the vertex into two equal parts, with the crossing bisector arcs shown inside the angle.
    Answer: Each part measures (i) 38°, (ii) 34°, (iii) 49°.
  • Q: Q4. Construct angles of the following measures with the help of protractor: (i) 96° (ii) 112° (iii) 128°. Divide these angles into four equal angles with the help of compasses.
    Ans: To divide an angle into four equal angles, bisect it, then bisect each half again.
    Part 1 — with a protractor: Draw each angle with a protractor: (i) 96°, (ii) 112°, (iii) 128°. Call a given angle ∠ABC with vertex B.
    Part 2 — dividing into four (same method for each angle):
    Step 1: With B as centre, draw an arc cutting the two arms of ∠ABC at K and L.
    Step 2: With L and K as centres and radius more than half of LK, draw arcs cutting each other at D. Join B to D; BD bisects ∠ABC and cuts arc KL at M.
    Step 3: Bisect the first half: with L and M as centres, draw arcs of suitable radius cutting each other at F; join B to F.
    Step 4: Bisect the second half: with M and K as centres, draw arcs of suitable radius cutting each other at E; join B to E.
    Step 5: Rays BE, BD and BF divide ∠ABC into four equal angles.
    Measure of each of the four parts = given angle ÷ 4:
    (i) 96° ÷ 4 = 24°
    (ii) 112° ÷ 4 = 28°
    (iii) 128° ÷ 4 = 32°
    Finished figure: Each angle has three inside rays from the vertex, making four equal openings, with the bisection arcs shown.
    Answer: Each of the four equal angles measures (i) 24°, (ii) 28°, (iii) 32°.
  • Q: Q5. Construct angles of the following measures by using compasses and ruler only: (i) 150° (ii) 165° (iii) 135° (iv) 105°
    Ans: Basic steps used (compasses and ruler only): 60° — draw ray BC, with B as centre draw an arc cutting BC at D, with D as centre and the same radius cut that arc at E; ray BE makes 60° with BC. Repeating the same arc-step gives 120°. 90° — construct 60°, then an adjacent 60° (120° in all), and bisect the second 60°; the bisector makes 60° + 30° = 90° with BC. Any angle below is then got by bisecting the angle between two rays already constructed.
    (i) 150° = 120° + half of 60°:
    Step 1: Draw ray BC.
    Step 2: At B, construct two consecutive 60° angles on the same arc, giving rays at 60° and 120° from BC.
    Step 3: The ray opposite to BC (the straight line through B) makes 180° with BC. Bisect the angle between the 120° ray and this straight line (180° − 120° = 60°, half = 30°).
    Step 4: The bisector ray, say BA, is the required ray.
    Finished figure (i): From B on base BC, rays stand at 60°, 120°, 150° and 180° (straight line); the angle between BA and BC is 150°.
    Answer: (i) 120° + 30° = 150°.
    (ii) 165° = 150° + half of 30°:
    Step 1: Draw ray BC and construct 150° at B as in (i), giving ray BA at 150°.
    Step 2: Bisect the angle between ray BA (150°) and the straight line (180°); this angle is 30°, so its bisector is 15° from each.
    Step 3: The bisector ray, say BD, is the required ray.
    Finished figure (ii): From B on base BC, rays stand at 60°, 120°, 150°, 165° and 180°; the angle between BD and BC is 165°, lying 15° short of the straight line.
    Answer: (ii) 180° − 15° = 165°.
    (iii) 135° = 90° + half of 90°:
    Step 1: Draw ray BC and construct 90° at B by compasses, giving a vertical ray.
    Step 2: Bisect the angle between this 90° ray and the straight line (180°); this angle is 90°, so its bisector is 45° from each.
    Step 3: The bisector ray, say BA, is the required ray.
    Finished figure (iii): From B on base BC, rays stand at 90° (vertical), 135° and 180° (straight line); the angle between BA and BC is 135°.
    Answer: (iii) 90° + 45° = 135°.
    (iv) 105° = 90° + half of 30°:
    Step 1: Draw ray BC and construct at B the rays at 60°, 90° and 120° as in the basic steps.
    Step 2: Bisect the angle between the 90° ray and the 120° ray; this angle is 30°, so its bisector is 15° from each.
    Step 3: The bisector ray, say BA, is the required ray.
    Finished figure (iv): From B on base BC, rays stand at 60°, 90°, 105° and 120°; the angle between BA and BC is 105°.
    Answer: (iv) 90° + 15° = 105°.

Exercise 10.3

  • Q: Q1. Construct △ABC, when: (i) mAB = 7cm, mBC = 3cm and mCA = 6cm (ii) mAB = 4.5cm, mBC = 3.5cm and mCA = 2.5cm
    Ans: SSS construction. First check the triangle rule: the sum of any two sides must be greater than the third side.
    (i) 3 + 6 = 9 > 7, 7 + 3 = 10 > 6, 7 + 6 = 13 > 3 — construction is possible.
    Step 1: Draw line segment AB = 7cm with a ruler.
    Step 2: With B as centre and radius BC = 3cm, draw an arc above AB.
    Step 3: With A as centre and radius CA = 6cm, draw an arc cutting the arc of Step 2 at C.
    Step 4: Join C to A and C to B.
    Finished figure (i): Triangle ABC with base AB = 7cm, side BC = 3cm on the right and side CA = 6cm on the left, the two arcs crossing at vertex C.
    (ii) 3.5 + 2.5 = 6.0 > 4.5, 4.5 + 2.5 = 7.0 > 3.5, 4.5 + 3.5 = 8.0 > 2.5 — construction is possible.
    Step 1: Draw line segment AB = 4.5cm with a ruler.
    Step 2: With B as centre and radius BC = 3.5cm, draw an arc above AB.
    Step 3: With A as centre and radius CA = 2.5cm, draw an arc cutting the arc of Step 2 at C.
    Step 4: Join C to A and C to B.
    Finished figure (ii): Triangle ABC with base AB = 4.5cm, side BC = 3.5cm and side CA = 2.5cm, vertex C at the crossing of the two arcs.
    Answer: △ABC is constructed in both parts by SSS.
  • Q: Q2. Construct △PQR, when: (i) mPQ = 5cm, m∠Q = 45° and mQR = 4cm (ii) mPQ = 5.3cm, m∠P = 60° and mPR = 4.2cm
    Ans: SAS construction: two sides and the angle between them are given.
    (i) Sides PQ and QR with included ∠Q = 45°:
    Step 1: Draw line segment PQ = 5cm with a ruler.
    Step 2: At Q, construct ∠PQX = 45° (construct 90° and bisect it, or use a protractor).
    Step 3: With Q as centre and radius QR = 4cm, draw an arc cutting ray QX at R.
    Step 4: Join R to P.
    Finished figure (i): Triangle PQR with base PQ = 5cm, ∠Q = 45° at the right-hand base vertex, side QR = 4cm rising from Q to R, and side PR joining R back to P.
    (ii) Sides PQ and PR with included ∠P = 60°:
    Step 1: Draw line segment PQ = 5.3cm with a ruler.
    Step 2: At P, construct ∠QPX = 60° with compasses (arc from P cutting PQ, then same radius from that point cutting the arc).
    Step 3: With P as centre and radius PR = 4.2cm, draw an arc cutting ray PX at R.
    Step 4: Join R to Q.
    Finished figure (ii): Triangle PQR with base PQ = 5.3cm, ∠P = 60° at the left-hand base vertex, side PR = 4.2cm rising from P to R, and side RQ joining R back to Q.
    Answer: △PQR is constructed in both parts by SAS.
  • Q: Q3. Construct △KLM, when: (i) mLM = 5.2cm, m∠L = 45° and m∠M = 30° (ii) mKL = 4.6cm, m∠K = 90° and m∠L = 60°
    Ans: ASA construction: two angles and the side between them are given.
    (i) Side LM with angles at L and M:
    Step 1: Draw line segment LM = 5.2cm with a ruler.
    Step 2: At L, construct an angle of 45° with the side LM (construct 90° and bisect it, or use a protractor) and draw the ray.
    Step 3: At M, construct an angle of 30° with the side ML (construct 60° and bisect it, or use a protractor) and draw the ray.
    Step 4: The two rays meet at K. Join is already complete: K is the third vertex.
    Finished figure (i): Triangle KLM with base LM = 5.2cm, ∠L = 45°, ∠M = 30°, and vertex K above the base where the two rays cross. The third angle is ∠K = 180° − 45° − 30° = 105°.
    (ii) Side KL with angles at K and L:
    Step 1: Draw line segment KL = 4.6cm with a ruler.
    Step 2: At K, construct a right angle of 90° with the side KL and draw the ray.
    Step 3: At L, construct an angle of 60° with the side LK with compasses and draw the ray.
    Step 4: The two rays meet at M.
    Finished figure (ii): Triangle KLM with base KL = 4.6cm, a right angle ∠K = 90° at the left-hand vertex, ∠L = 60°, and vertex M where the two rays cross. The third angle is ∠M = 180° − 90° − 60° = 30°.
    Answer: △KLM is constructed in both parts by ASA.
  • Q: Q4. Construct △XYZ, when: (i) mXY = 3cm, mXZ = 5cm and m∠Y = 90° (ii) mYZ = 6.5cm, mXY = 2.5cm and m∠X = 90°
    Ans: RHS construction: a right angle, the hypotenuse and one side are given. The hypotenuse is always opposite the right angle.
    (i) Right angle at Y, so XZ is the hypotenuse = 5cm, and XY = 3cm:
    Step 1: Draw line segment XY = 3cm with a ruler.
    Step 2: At Y, construct ∠XYL = 90° and draw ray YL.
    Step 3: With X as centre and radius XZ = 5cm (the hypotenuse), draw an arc cutting ray YL at Z.
    Step 4: Join Z to X.
    Finished figure (i): Right-angled triangle XYZ with the right angle at Y (bottom right), base XY = 3cm, vertical side YZ, and slanted hypotenuse XZ = 5cm from X up to Z.
    (ii) Right angle at X, so YZ is the hypotenuse = 6.5cm, and XY = 2.5cm:
    Step 1: Draw line segment XY = 2.5cm with a ruler.
    Step 2: At X, construct ∠YX L = 90° (an angle of 90° at X on XY) and draw the ray from X.
    Step 3: With Y as centre and radius YZ = 6.5cm (the hypotenuse), draw an arc cutting the ray of Step 2 at Z.
    Step 4: Join Z to Y.
    Finished figure (ii): Right-angled triangle XYZ with the right angle at X, short side XY = 2.5cm, side XZ along the ray from X, and slanted hypotenuse YZ = 6.5cm from Y up to Z.
    Answer: △XYZ is constructed in both parts by RHS.

mcqs.q: An angle of 65° is copied using compasses and ruler only. What is the measure of the copied angle?
mcqs.why: Copying an angle with compasses and ruler makes an angle equal in measure to the given angle. The arc from centre B and the chord distance PQ are transferred unchanged, so the copied angle measures the same as the original: 65 degrees.

mcqs.q: An angle of 42° is doubled using compasses and ruler. What is the measure of the constructed angle?
mcqs.why: Doubling means stepping the same chord distance twice along one arc. Calculation: double of 42 degrees = 2 x 42 degrees. Step 1: 2 x 42 = 84. So the constructed angle measures 84 degrees.

mcqs.q: An angle of 76° is bisected with compasses. What is the measure of each part?
mcqs.why: A bisector divides an angle into two equal parts, so each part = given angle divided by 2. Step 1: Given angle = 76 degrees. Step 2: 76 degrees divided by 2 = 38 degrees. Each part measures 38 degrees.

mcqs.q: An angle of 98° is bisected with compasses. What is the measure of each part?
mcqs.why: Each part after bisection = given angle divided by 2. Step 1: Given angle = 98 degrees. Step 2: 98 divided by 2 = 49. So each of the two equal parts measures 49 degrees.

mcqs.q: An angle of 112° is divided into four equal angles with compasses. What is the measure of each part?
mcqs.why: To divide into four equal angles, bisect the angle and then bisect each half again. Each part = given angle divided by 4. Step 1: Given angle = 112 degrees. Step 2: 112 divided by 4 = 28. Each part measures 28 degrees.

mcqs.q: Using compasses and ruler only, 135° is constructed as 90° plus half of 90°. What is half of 90° in this construction?
mcqs.why: Step fact: construct 90 degrees at B, then bisect the angle between the 90 degree ray and the straight line (180 degrees). That angle is 180 - 90 = 90 degrees, and its bisector is 90 divided by 2 = 45 degrees from each side, giving 90 + 45 = 135 degrees.

mcqs.q: Using compasses and ruler only, 105° is constructed as 90° plus half of 30°. What is half of 30° in this construction?
mcqs.why: Step fact: the angle between the 90 degree ray and the 120 degree ray is 120 - 90 = 30 degrees. Bisecting it gives 30 divided by 2 = 15 degrees from each ray. So 105 degrees = 90 degrees + 15 degrees.

mcqs.q: A triangle is constructed when all three side lengths AB, BC and CA are given. Which construction is this?
mcqs.why: When the three sides are given, the triangle is built by the SSS construction: draw one side with a ruler, then draw arcs with radii equal to the other two sides from its ends; the arcs cross at the third vertex. Before constructing, check that the sum of any two sides is greater than the third side.

mcqs.q: In triangle KLM, side LM = 5.2 cm with angle L = 45° and angle M = 30°. What is the measure of angle K?
mcqs.why: The three angles of a triangle add to 180 degrees. Step 1: Angle L + angle M = 45 + 30 = 75 degrees. Step 2: Angle K = 180 - 75 = 105 degrees. This is the ASA case: two angles and the side between them are given.

mcqs.q: In triangle XYZ the right angle is at Y, with XY = 3 cm and XZ = 5 cm. Which side is the hypotenuse, and what is its length?
mcqs.why: In the RHS construction the hypotenuse is always opposite the right angle. The right angle is at Y, so the side opposite Y is XZ. Its given length is 5 cm, drawn as an arc from X cutting the ray from Y at Z.

lessons.title: Review Exercise 10
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Sum segments are found by adding: mKL = mAB + mCD; remainders after cutting off are found by subtracting.
  • The right bisector of a 5.8 cm segment gives two halves of 2.9 cm each and meets the segment at 90°.
  • For an 80° angle: the copy is 80°, the double is 160°, each bisected part is 40°, and each of four equal parts is 20°.
  • Angles 22½° and 67½° are constructible by repeated bisection: 90° → 45° → 22½°, and 67½° = 45° + 22½°.
  • In an RHS triangle the hypotenuse is opposite the right angle; e.g. with right angle at B, AC is the hypotenuse.

Review Exercise 10

  • Q: Q1. Draw AB and CD such that mAB = 3.6cm and mCD = 1.9cm. Draw KL where mKL = mAB + mCD. Measure the length of KL.
    Ans: Step 1: With a ruler draw AB = 3.6cm and CD = 1.9cm.
    Step 2: Draw a line and take a point K on it.
    Step 3: With K as centre and radius equal to AB (3.6cm), draw an arc cutting the line at a point, say P, so KP = 3.6cm.
    Step 4: With P as centre and radius equal to CD (1.9cm), draw an arc cutting the line at L, so PL = 1.9cm.
    Step 5: Measure KL with a ruler.
    Calculation: mKL = 3.6cm + 1.9cm = 5.5cm.
    Finished figure: K, P, L lie in order on one straight line; KP is marked 3.6cm and PL is marked 1.9cm.
    Answer: mKL = 5.5cm.
  • Q: Q2. Draw XY 5.8cm long. Cut off XA where mXA = 2.6cm. Measure the length of AY.
    Ans: Step 1: With a ruler draw XY = 5.8cm.
    Step 2: With X as centre and radius 2.6cm, draw an arc cutting XY at A, so XA = 2.6cm is cut off.
    Step 3: AY is the remaining part; measure it with a ruler.
    Calculation: mAY = mXY − mXA = 5.8cm − 2.6cm = 3.2cm.
    Finished figure: Segment XY of 5.8cm with point A on it 2.6cm from X; AY runs from A to Y.
    Answer: mAY = 3.2cm.
  • Q: Q3. Draw KL such that mKL = 6.4cm. Cut off KT where mKT = 3cm. Measure the length of TL.
    Ans: Step 1: With a ruler draw KL = 6.4cm.
    Step 2: With K as centre and radius 3cm, draw an arc cutting KL at T, so KT = 3cm is cut off.
    Step 3: TL is the remaining part; measure it with a ruler.
    Calculation: mTL = mKL − mKT = 6.4cm − 3cm = 3.4cm.
    Finished figure: Segment KL of 6.4cm with point T on it 3cm from K; TL runs from T to L.
    Answer: mTL = 3.4cm.
  • Q: Q4. Draw AB 5.8cm long. Draw its right bisector with the help of ruler and compasses only.
    Ans: Step 1: With a ruler draw AB = 5.8cm.
    Step 2: With A as centre and radius more than half of AB (more than 2.9cm), draw arcs above and below AB.
    Step 3: With B as centre and the same radius, draw arcs cutting the first arcs at P (above) and Q (below).
    Step 4: Join P to Q with a ruler. Line PQ cuts AB at its midpoint R.
    Step 5: PQ is the right bisector: PQ ⊥ AB and AR = RB = 5.8 ÷ 2 = 2.9cm.
    Finished figure: Horizontal segment AB = 5.8cm crossed at its midpoint R by vertical line PQ, with crossing arcs shown at P above and Q below.
  • Q: Q5. Draw AB 4.8cm long. Take a point C on AB such that mAC = 1.6cm. At C, draw a perpendicular to AB by using ruler and compasses only.
    Ans: Step 1: With a ruler draw AB = 4.8cm.
    Step 2: With A as centre and radius 1.6cm, draw a small arc cutting AB at C, so AC = 1.6cm (and CB = 4.8 − 1.6 = 3.2cm).
    Step 3: With C as centre and any suitable radius, draw arcs cutting AB at P on the A-side and Q on the B-side, so CP = CQ.
    Step 4: With P as centre and radius more than half of PQ, draw an arc above AB.
    Step 5: With Q as centre and the same radius, draw an arc cutting the arc of Step 4 at R.
    Step 6: Join C to R. CR is the required perpendicular, so CR ⊥ AB at C.
    Finished figure: Segment AB = 4.8cm with point C marked 1.6cm from A, equal points P and Q on either side of C, and a vertical line through C up to R where the arcs cross.
  • Q: Q6. Draw AB 3.9 cm long. Take a point C outside AB and draw perpendicular to AB from C. (use ruler and compass only).
    Ans: Step 1: With a ruler draw AB = 3.9cm and take a point C outside (above) AB.
    Step 2: With C as centre and a suitable radius large enough to reach AB, draw an arc cutting AB at P and Q.
    Step 3: With P as centre and a suitable radius, draw an arc below AB.
    Step 4: With Q as centre and the same radius, draw an arc cutting the arc of Step 3 at S.
    Step 5: Join C to S with a ruler; line CS cuts AB at R.
    Step 6: CR is the required perpendicular, so CR ⊥ AB.
    Finished figure: Segment AB = 3.9cm with point C above it, a long arc from C crossing AB at P and Q, two crossing arcs below AB at S, and the line from C through R on AB down to S at right angles to AB.
  • Q: Q7. With the help of protractor, draw ∠ABC such that m∠ABC = 80°. Using ruler and compasses only (i) Construct an angle equal in measure to ∠ABC. (ii) Construct an angle twice in measure of ∠ABC. (iii) Draw the bisector of ∠ABC. (iv) Divide ∠ABC into four equal angles. Verify the measures with the help of protractor.
    Ans: First draw the given angle: draw ray BC, place the protractor centre at B with its base along BC, mark 80°, and join B to the mark to get ray BA, so ∠ABC = 80°.
    (i) Equal angle (copying with compasses):
    Step 1: With centre B, draw an arc cutting BC and BA at two points.
    Step 2: Draw a new ray, with the same radius draw an arc from its end point cutting the ray at one point.
    Step 3: With that point as centre and radius equal to the distance between the two points on the first arc, cut the new arc; join the end point to the cutting point.
    Finished figure (i): A new angle identical in opening to ∠ABC.
    Answer (i): The copied angle measures 80° (verified by protractor).
    (ii) Twice the angle:
    Step 1: With centre B, draw an arc cutting BC and BA.
    Step 2: On a new ray, draw the same arc; step the chord distance of ∠ABC along this arc twice, in two consecutive steps, from the point where the arc cuts the ray.
    Step 3: Join the vertex to the end of the second step.
    Finished figure (ii): An angle with two equal consecutive arc-steps marked on one big arc.
    Answer (ii): 2 × 80° = 160° (verified by protractor).
    (iii) Bisector:
    Step 1: With B as centre, draw an arc cutting BA and BC at two points.
    Step 2: With those two points as centres and radius more than half the distance between them, draw arcs inside the angle cutting each other at a point D.
    Step 3: Join B to D. BD bisects ∠ABC.
    Answer (iii): Each part = 80° ÷ 2 = 40° (verified by protractor).
    (iv) Four equal angles: Bisect ∠ABC as in (iii), then bisect each 40° half by the same method, giving three inside rays from B.
    Answer (iv): Each part = 80° ÷ 4 = 20° (verified by protractor).
  • Q: Q8. Using ruler and compasses only, construct △ABC, where (i) mAB = 6.5cm, mBC = 4cm and mCA = 3.5cm (ii) mBC = 4.4cm, m∠B = 22 1/2° and m∠C = 67 1/2° (iii) mAB = 4.5cm, m∠B = 90° and mAC = 5.9cm
    Ans: (i) SSS — three sides given. Check: 4 + 3.5 = 7.5 > 6.5, so construction is possible.
    Step 1: Draw line segment AB = 6.5cm.
    Step 2: With B as centre and radius BC = 4cm, draw an arc above AB.
    Step 3: With A as centre and radius CA = 3.5cm, draw an arc cutting the arc of Step 2 at C.
    Step 4: Join C to A and C to B.
    Finished figure (i): Triangle ABC with base AB = 6.5cm, BC = 4cm, CA = 3.5cm, vertex C at the crossing of the two arcs.
    (ii) ASA — side BC with its two end angles given. Note: 22 1/2° = half of 45° and 67 1/2° = 90° − 22 1/2°, both constructible by compasses by repeated bisection (90° → 45° → 22 1/2°; 67 1/2° = 45° + 22 1/2°).
    Step 1: Draw line segment BC = 4.4cm.
    Step 2: At B, construct an angle of 22 1/2° with BC: construct 90°, bisect to 45°, bisect again to 22 1/2°, and draw the ray.
    Step 3: At C, construct an angle of 67 1/2° with CB: construct 45° and add an adjacent 22 1/2° (or construct 90° and subtract 22 1/2°), and draw the ray.
    Step 4: The two rays meet at A.
    Finished figure (ii): Triangle ABC with base BC = 4.4cm, ∠B = 22 1/2°, ∠C = 67 1/2°, and vertex A where the rays cross. The third angle is ∠A = 180° − 22 1/2° − 67 1/2° = 90°.
    (iii) RHS — right angle at B, hypotenuse AC and one side AB given (AC is opposite ∠B = 90°, so AC is the hypotenuse).
    Step 1: Draw line segment AB = 4.5cm.
    Step 2: At B, construct ∠AB L = 90° with compasses and draw ray BL.
    Step 3: With A as centre and radius AC = 5.9cm (the hypotenuse), draw an arc cutting ray BL at C.
    Step 4: Join C to A.
    Finished figure (iii): Right-angled triangle ABC with the right angle at B, side AB = 4.5cm along the base, side BC vertical along BL, and slanted hypotenuse AC = 5.9cm from A up to C.
    Answer: △ABC is constructed in all three parts using ruler and compasses only.

mcqs.q: AB = 3.6 cm and CD = 1.9 cm. KL is drawn with mKL = mAB + mCD. What is mKL?
mcqs.why: mKL = mAB + mCD. Step 1: Substitute: mKL = 3.6 cm + 1.9 cm, with KP = 3.6 cm and PL = 1.9 cm laid end to end. Step 2: Add: 3.6 + 1.9 = 5.5. So mKL = 5.5 cm.

mcqs.q: XY is 5.8 cm long and XA = 2.6 cm is cut off from it. What is the length of AY?
mcqs.why: mAY = mXY - mXA. Step 1: mXY = 5.8 cm and mXA = 2.6 cm. Step 2: Subtract: 5.8 - 2.6 = 3.2. So the remaining part AY measures 3.2 cm.

mcqs.q: KL is 6.4 cm long and KT = 3 cm is cut off from it. What is the length of TL?
mcqs.why: mTL = mKL - mKT. Step 1: mKL = 6.4 cm and mKT = 3 cm. Step 2: Subtract: 6.4 - 3 = 3.4. So the remaining part TL measures 3.4 cm.

mcqs.q: AB is 5.8 cm long. Its right bisector PQ cuts AB at midpoint R. What are AR and RB?
mcqs.why: A right bisector cuts a segment into two equal halves at 90 degrees. Step 1: AB = 5.8 cm. Step 2: Each half = 5.8 divided by 2 = 2.9 cm. So AR = RB = 2.9 cm and PQ is perpendicular to AB.

mcqs.q: AB is 4.8 cm long and point C is on AB with AC = 1.6 cm. What is the length of CB?
mcqs.why: CB = AB - AC. Step 1: AB = 4.8 cm and AC = 1.6 cm. Step 2: Subtract: 4.8 - 1.6 = 3.2. So CB = 3.2 cm. At C a perpendicular CR is then drawn with ruler and compasses.

mcqs.q: Triangle ABC has base BC = 4.4 cm, angle B = 22½° and angle C = 67½°. What is the measure of angle A?
mcqs.why: The angles of a triangle add to 180 degrees. Step 1: Angle B + angle C = 22.5 + 67.5 = 90 degrees. Step 2: Angle A = 180 - 90 = 90 degrees. This is an ASA construction with side BC and its two end angles given.

mcqs.q: Angle ABC measures 80°. An angle equal to it is constructed with ruler and compasses only. What does the constructed angle measure?
mcqs.why: Copying an angle transfers the same arc and chord distance, so the new angle is equal to the given angle. Given angle ABC = 80 degrees, so the copied angle also measures 80 degrees, verified with the protractor.

mcqs.q: Angle ABC measures 80°. An angle twice its measure is constructed. What is the measure of the new angle?
mcqs.why: Twice the angle = 2 x given angle. Step 1: Given angle = 80 degrees. Step 2: 2 x 80 = 160. The chord distance is stepped twice along one arc, so the constructed angle measures 160 degrees.

mcqs.q: Angle ABC measures 80°. Its bisector is drawn with compasses. What is the measure of each part?
mcqs.why: A bisector divides an angle into two equal parts. Each part = given angle divided by 2. Step 1: Given angle = 80 degrees. Step 2: 80 divided by 2 = 40. Each part measures 40 degrees.

mcqs.q: Angle ABC measures 80° and is divided into four equal angles. What is the measure of each part?
mcqs.why: Dividing into four is done by bisecting the angle and then bisecting each half. Each part = given angle divided by 4. Step 1: Given angle = 80 degrees. Step 2: 80 divided by 4 = 20. Each part measures 20 degrees.

lessons.title: Exercise 11.1
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Area of rectangle = length × breadth; a missing side = Area ÷ known side.
  • Perimeter of rectangle = 2(length + breadth); Perimeter of square = 4 × side; Area of square = side × side.
  • Cost problems: first find the area, then multiply by the rate (converting the rate per 100 m² into units when needed).
  • Remaining area = area of the whole shape minus the area taken by the parts inside it.
  • Area of triangle = ½ × base × height, used for the corner triangles of the table mat (each 0.5 cm²).

Exercise 11.1

  • Q: 1. Find the missing dimension in each rectangle. (i) A rectangle drawn tilted like a diamond, with one side 15 cm, the other side marked l, and Area = 270 cm (as printed). (ii) A rectangle with side 16 m, the top side marked w, and Area = 176 m (as printed). (iii) A rectangle with width 11 m, the top side marked l, and Perimeter = 70 m.
    Ans: Formula: Area of rectangle = length × breadth, so missing side = Area ÷ known side.
    (i) l = 270 ÷ 15
    l = 18
    Answer: l = 18 cm.
    (ii) w = 176 ÷ 16
    w = 11
    Answer: w = 11 m.
    (iii) Formula: Perimeter of rectangle = 2(l + w)
    70 = 2(l + 11)
    70 = 2l + 22
    2l = 70 − 22 = 48
    l = 48 ÷ 2 = 24
    Answer: l = 24 m.
    Note: In (i) and (ii) the book prints the area unit without the square sign; the areas are 270 cm² and 176 m².
  • Q: 2. Find the perimeter and area of each figure. (i) A rectangle 7 yd long and 1 yd wide. (ii) A square with side 1 in.
    Ans: (i) Formula: Perimeter of rectangle = 2(l + w)
    P = 2(7 + 1) = 2 × 8 = 16 yd
    Formula: Area of rectangle = length × width
    A = 7 × 1 = 7
    Answer: Perimeter = 16 yd, Area = 7 yd² (square yards).
    (ii) Formula: Perimeter of square = 4 × side
    P = 4 × 1 = 4 in
    Formula: Area of square = side × side
    A = 1 × 1 = 1
    Answer: Perimeter = 4 in, Area = 1 in² (square inch).
  • Q: 3. Find the perimeter and area of squares having one side equal to: (i) 20 cm (ii) 3.6 m (iii) 59 cm
    Ans: Formula: Perimeter of square = 4 × side; Area of square = side × side.
    (i) P = 4 × 20 = 80 cm
    A = 20 × 20 = 400 cm²
    Answer: Perimeter = 80 cm, Area = 400 cm².
    (ii) P = 4 × 3.6 = 14.4 m
    A = 3.6 × 3.6 = 12.96 m²
    Answer: Perimeter = 14.4 m, Area = 12.96 m².
    (iii) P = 4 × 59 = 236 cm
    A = 59 × 59 = 3481 cm²
    Answer: Perimeter = 236 cm, Area = 3481 cm².
  • Q: 4. Find the perimeter and area of rectangles having: (i) Length = 9 cm, Breadth = 5 cm (ii) Length = 40.2 m, Breadth = 27.8 m
    Ans: Formula: Perimeter of rectangle = 2(l + b); Area of rectangle = l × b.
    (i) P = 2(9 + 5) = 2 × 14 = 28 cm
    A = 9 × 5 = 45 cm²
    Answer: Perimeter = 28 cm, Area = 45 cm².
    (ii) P = 2(40.2 + 27.8) = 2 × 68 = 136 m
    A = 40.2 × 27.8 = 1117.56 m²
    Answer: Perimeter = 136 m, Area = 1117.56 m².
  • Q: 5. Assembly ground of a school is 150 m long and 100 m wide. Find the cost of its brick flooring if the rate is Rs. 1500 per 100 m².
    Ans: Formula: Area of rectangle = length × width
    Area of the ground = 150 × 100 = 15000 m²
    Number of 100 m² units = 15000 ÷ 100 = 150
    Cost = 150 × 1500 = 225000
    Answer: The cost of brick flooring is Rs. 225,000.
  • Q: 6. A room having 5 m length and 3.5 m breadth is to be carpeted. Find the total cost, if the rate is 545 rupees per square meter.
    Ans: Formula: Area of rectangle = length × breadth
    Area of the room = 5 × 3.5 = 17.5 m²
    Total cost = 17.5 × 545 = 9537.5
    Answer: The total cost of carpeting is Rs. 9,537.50.
  • Q: 7. A gardener made 6 square shaped flower beds in a rectangular garden having length 20 m and breadth 6 m. If the side of each flower bed is 2.5 m, find the remaining area of the garden.
    Ans: Formula: Area of rectangle = length × breadth
    Area of the garden = 20 × 6 = 120 m²
    Formula: Area of square = side × side
    Area of one flower bed = 2.5 × 2.5 = 6.25 m²
    Area of 6 flower beds = 6 × 6.25 = 37.5 m²
    Remaining area = 120 − 37.5 = 82.5 m²
    Answer: The remaining area of the garden is 82.5 m².
  • Q: 8. The illustration shows a table mat which has a decorative pattern. The mat is a square divided into a 6 × 6 grid of small squares. The coloured parts are: 4 small squares standing alone, 4 small squares joined in a 2 × 2 block in the centre, and a right-angled triangle in each corner whose two equal sides are each equal to the side of one small square. If each coloured square has an area of 1 cm², can you find: a) the total area which is coloured? b) the area of the whole mat?
    Ans: Each small square has area 1 cm², so the side of each small square is 1 cm.
    a) Coloured squares = 4 alone + 4 in the centre = 8 squares
    Area of the 8 squares = 8 × 1 = 8 cm²
    Formula: Area of triangle = 1/2 × base × height
    Each corner triangle has base 1 cm and height 1 cm, so its area = 1/2 × 1 × 1 = 0.5 cm²
    Area of 4 corner triangles = 4 × 0.5 = 2 cm²
    Total coloured area = 8 + 2 = 10 cm²
    Answer: a) The total coloured area is 10 cm².
    b) The whole mat is 6 small squares long and 6 small squares wide.
    Side of the mat = 6 × 1 = 6 cm
    Formula: Area of square = side × side
    Area of the whole mat = 6 × 6 = 36 cm²
    Answer: b) The area of the whole mat is 36 cm².

mcqs.q: A rectangle has area 270 cm² and one side 15 cm. What is the length of the other side?
mcqs.why: Area of rectangle = length x breadth, so the missing side = Area divided by the known side. Step 1: Area = 270 square cm and known side = 15 cm. Step 2: l = 270 divided by 15 = 18. So the other side is 18 cm. Note: the book prints the area unit without the square sign; it should be cm squared.

mcqs.q: A rectangle has width 11 m and perimeter 70 m. What is its length?
mcqs.why: Perimeter of rectangle = 2(length + breadth). Step 1: 70 = 2(l + 11), so 70 = 2l + 22. Step 2: 2l = 70 - 22 = 48. Step 3: l = 48 divided by 2 = 24. So the length is 24 m.

mcqs.q: Find the perimeter of a rectangle 7 yd long and 1 yd wide.
mcqs.why: Perimeter of rectangle = 2(length + width). Step 1: length + width = 7 + 1 = 8 yd. Step 2: P = 2 x 8 = 16 yd. The area for reference is Area of rectangle = length x width = 7 x 1 = 7 square yards.

mcqs.q: Find the area of a square with side 3.6 m.
mcqs.why: Area of square = side x side. Step 1: side = 3.6 m. Step 2: A = 3.6 x 3.6 = 12.96 square metres. For reference, Perimeter of square = 4 x side = 4 x 3.6 = 14.4 m.

mcqs.q: Find the perimeter of a rectangle with length 40.2 m and breadth 27.8 m.
mcqs.why: Perimeter of rectangle = 2(length + breadth). Step 1: length + breadth = 40.2 + 27.8 = 68 m. Step 2: P = 2 x 68 = 136 m. For reference, Area of rectangle = length x breadth = 40.2 x 27.8 = 1117.56 square metres.

mcqs.q: An assembly ground is 150 m long and 100 m wide. Brick flooring costs Rs. 1500 per 100 m². What is the total cost?
mcqs.why: Area of rectangle = length x width. Step 1: Area = 150 x 100 = 15000 square metres. Step 2: Number of 100 square metre units = 15000 divided by 100 = 150. Step 3: Cost = 150 x 1500 = 225000. So the cost is Rs. 225,000.

mcqs.q: A room is 5 m long and 3.5 m broad. Carpeting costs Rs. 545 per square metre. What is the total cost?
mcqs.why: Area of rectangle = length x breadth. Step 1: Area = 5 x 3.5 = 17.5 square metres. Step 2: Total cost = 17.5 x 545 = 9537.5. So the total cost of carpeting is Rs. 9,537.50.

mcqs.q: A rectangular garden is 20 m by 6 m. Six square flower beds of side 2.5 m are made in it. What area of the garden remains?
mcqs.why: Area of rectangle = length x breadth, so garden area = 20 x 6 = 120 square metres. Area of square = side x side, so one bed = 2.5 x 2.5 = 6.25 square metres. Step 3: Six beds = 6 x 6.25 = 37.5. Step 4: Remaining = 120 - 37.5 = 82.5 square metres.

mcqs.q: A square table mat is a 6 by 6 grid of small squares. Coloured parts are 8 small squares of area 1 cm² each plus 4 corner right-angled triangles with base 1 cm and height 1 cm. What is the total coloured area?
mcqs.why: Area of the 8 squares = 8 x 1 = 8 square cm. Area of triangle = one-half x base x height, so each corner triangle = one-half x 1 x 1 = 0.5 square cm. Step 3: Four triangles = 4 x 0.5 = 2 square cm. Step 4: Total coloured area = 8 + 2 = 10 square cm.

mcqs.q: The same table mat is 6 small squares long and 6 wide, each small square having side 1 cm. What is the area of the whole mat?
mcqs.why: Side of the mat = 6 x 1 cm = 6 cm, since each small square has area 1 square cm and side 1 cm. Area of square = side x side. Step 1: A = 6 x 6 = 36. So the area of the whole mat is 36 square cm.

lessons.title: Exercise 11.2
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Shaded or border area = area of the outer shape minus area of the inner shape.
  • Road outside: add the width on both sides (side + width + width); road inside: subtract the width on both sides.
  • Cost = area of the road or pavement × rate per square metre.
  • For two crossing roads, add both road areas and subtract the overlapping square (width × width) once, because it is counted twice.

Exercise 11.2

  • Q: 1. Find the area of the shaded part of each shape. (i) A rectangular frame: the outer rectangle is 15 cm by 8 cm and the inner unshaded rectangle is 12 cm by 5 cm. (ii) A rectangular frame: the outer rectangle is 12 cm by 6 cm and the inner unshaded rectangle is 10 cm by 4 cm.
    Ans: Method: Area of shaded part = Area of outer rectangle − Area of inner rectangle.
    Formula: Area of rectangle = length × width.
    (i) Outer area = 15 × 8 = 120 cm²
    Inner area = 12 × 5 = 60 cm²
    Shaded area = 120 − 60 = 60 cm²
    Answer: (i) 60 cm².
    (ii) Outer area = 12 × 6 = 72 cm²
    Inner area = 10 × 4 = 40 cm²
    Shaded area = 72 − 40 = 32 cm²
    Answer: (ii) 32 cm².
  • Q: 2. A square carpet of side length 3.9 m is laid in a room measuring 4 m by 4 m. Find the area of floor left uncovered.
    Ans: Formula: Area of square = side × side
    Area of the room floor = 4 × 4 = 16 m²
    Area of the carpet = 3.9 × 3.9 = 15.21 m²
    Uncovered area = 16 − 15.21 = 0.79 m²
    Answer: The area of floor left uncovered is 0.79 m².
  • Q: 3. A square shaped park is 170 m long. A road 6 m wide has been constructed along the outer side of the boundary. Find the area of the road.
    Ans: Formula: Area of square = side × side
    Area of the park = 170 × 170 = 28900 m²
    The road is outside, so the side of the outer square = 170 + 6 + 6 = 182 m
    Area of the outer square = 182 × 182 = 33124 m²
    Area of the road = 33124 − 28900 = 4224 m²
    Answer: The area of the road is 4224 m².
  • Q: 4. A park is of square shape and one side of the park is 275 m long. A road 9 m wide has been constructed along the inner side of the boundary. Find the area of the road.
    Ans: Formula: Area of square = side × side
    Area of the park = 275 × 275 = 75625 m²
    The road is inside, so the side of the inner square = 275 − 9 − 9 = 257 m
    Area of the inner square = 257 × 257 = 66049 m²
    Area of the road = 75625 − 66049 = 9576 m²
    Answer: The area of the road is 9576 m².
  • Q: 5. A rectangular park is 190 m long and 160 m wide. A road 8 m wide has been constructed along the outer side of the boundary. Find the area of the road.
    Ans: Formula: Area of rectangle = length × width
    Area of the park = 190 × 160 = 30400 m²
    The road is outside, so the length of the outer rectangle = 190 + 8 + 8 = 206 m
    Width of the outer rectangle = 160 + 8 + 8 = 176 m
    Area of the outer rectangle = 206 × 176 = 36256 m²
    Area of the road = 36256 − 30400 = 5856 m²
    Answer: The area of the road is 5856 m².
  • Q: 6. A pavement 4 m wide is constructed along the outer side of the boundary of a square shaped ground having its side of 13 m length. Find the cost of levelling the pavement at the rate of Rs. 1.25 per square meter.
    Ans: Formula: Area of square = side × side
    Area of the ground = 13 × 13 = 169 m²
    Side of the outer square = 13 + 4 + 4 = 21 m
    Area of the outer square = 21 × 21 = 441 m²
    Area of the pavement = 441 − 169 = 272 m²
    Cost of levelling = 272 × 1.25 = 340
    Answer: The area of the pavement is 272 m² and the cost of levelling it is Rs. 340.
  • Q: 7. A park is 110 m long and 96 m wide. In the middle of the park two roads 4 m wide parallel to its sides are constructed. Find the area of the roads.
    Ans: Formula: Area of rectangle = length × width
    Area of the road parallel to the length = 110 × 4 = 440 m²
    Area of the road parallel to the width = 96 × 4 = 384 m²
    The middle 4 m × 4 m square is counted twice, so subtract it once: 4 × 4 = 16 m²
    Area of the roads = 440 + 384 − 16 = 808 m²
    Answer: The area of the roads is 808 m².

mcqs.q: A rectangular frame has outer dimensions 15 cm by 8 cm and inner unshaded rectangle 12 cm by 5 cm. What is the area of the shaded part?
mcqs.why: Area of shaded part = Area of outer rectangle minus Area of inner rectangle, with Area of rectangle = length x width. Step 1: Outer area = 15 x 8 = 120 square cm. Step 2: Inner area = 12 x 5 = 60 square cm. Step 3: Shaded area = 120 - 60 = 60 square cm.

mcqs.q: A rectangular frame has outer dimensions 12 cm by 6 cm and inner unshaded rectangle 10 cm by 4 cm. What is the area of the shaded part?
mcqs.why: Area of shaded part = Area of outer rectangle minus Area of inner rectangle, with Area of rectangle = length x width. Step 1: Outer area = 12 x 6 = 72 square cm. Step 2: Inner area = 10 x 4 = 40 square cm. Step 3: Shaded area = 72 - 40 = 32 square cm.

mcqs.q: A square carpet of side 3.9 m is laid in a room 4 m by 4 m. What area of floor is left uncovered?
mcqs.why: Area of square = side x side. Step 1: Room floor area = 4 x 4 = 16 square metres. Step 2: Carpet area = 3.9 x 3.9 = 15.21 square metres. Step 3: Uncovered area = 16 - 15.21 = 0.79 square metres.

mcqs.q: A square park has side 170 m. A road 6 m wide is built outside along its boundary. What is the area of the road?
mcqs.why: Area of square = side x side. Step 1: Park area = 170 x 170 = 28900 square metres. Step 2: Outer side = 170 + 6 + 6 = 182 m, so outer area = 182 x 182 = 33124 square metres. Step 3: Road area = 33124 - 28900 = 4224 square metres.

mcqs.q: A square park has side 275 m. A road 9 m wide is built inside along its boundary. What is the side of the inner square left inside the road?
mcqs.why: For a road inside, subtract the road width from both sides. Step 1: Side of park = 275 m and road width = 9 m. Step 2: Inner side = 275 - 9 - 9 = 257 m. Its area is 257 x 257 = 66049 square metres, used to find the road area.

mcqs.q: For the same park of side 275 m with a 9 m wide road inside, what is the area of the road?
mcqs.why: Area of square = side x side. Step 1: Park area = 275 x 275 = 75625 square metres. Step 2: Inner side = 275 - 9 - 9 = 257 m, inner area = 257 x 257 = 66049 square metres. Step 3: Road area = 75625 - 66049 = 9576 square metres.

mcqs.q: A rectangular park is 190 m by 160 m. A road 8 m wide is built outside along its boundary. What is the area of the road?
mcqs.why: Area of rectangle = length x width. Step 1: Park area = 190 x 160 = 30400 square metres. Step 2: Outer length = 190 + 8 + 8 = 206 m and outer width = 160 + 8 + 8 = 176 m, outer area = 206 x 176 = 36256 square metres. Step 3: Road area = 36256 - 30400 = 5856 square metres.

mcqs.q: A pavement 4 m wide is built outside a square ground of side 13 m. What is the area of the pavement?
mcqs.why: Area of square = side x side. Step 1: Ground area = 13 x 13 = 169 square metres. Step 2: Outer side = 13 + 4 + 4 = 21 m, outer area = 21 x 21 = 441 square metres. Step 3: Pavement area = 441 - 169 = 272 square metres.

mcqs.q: The pavement in the previous case has area 272 m². Levelling costs Rs. 1.25 per square metre. What is the cost of levelling?
mcqs.why: Cost = area of pavement x rate per square metre. Step 1: Pavement area = 272 square metres, found as outer area 441 minus ground area 169. Step 2: Cost = 272 x 1.25 = 340. So the cost of levelling is Rs. 340.

mcqs.q: A park is 110 m long and 96 m wide. Two roads 4 m wide, parallel to its sides, cross in the middle. What is the total area of the roads?
mcqs.why: Area of rectangle = length x width. Step 1: Road along the length = 110 x 4 = 440 square metres. Step 2: Road along the width = 96 x 4 = 384 square metres. Step 3: The middle 4 x 4 = 16 square metres is counted twice, so subtract it once: 440 + 384 - 16 = 808 square metres.

lessons.title: Exercise 11.3
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Area of triangle = ½ × base × altitude.
  • Area of parallelogram = base × altitude.
  • Area of trapezium = ½ × altitude × (sum of parallel sides).
  • For cost or yield problems, first find the area with the shape formula, then multiply by the rate per square metre.

Exercise 11.3

  • Q: 1. Find the area of the following triangles: (i) base 10 cm, altitude 4 cm (ii) base 6 cm, altitude 6 cm (iii) base 12 cm, altitude 5 cm
    Ans: Formula: Area of triangle = 1/2 × base × altitude
    (i) A = 1/2 × 10 × 4 = 20 cm²
    (ii) A = 1/2 × 6 × 6 = 18 cm²
    (iii) A = 1/2 × 12 × 5 = 30 cm²
    Answer: (i) 20 cm², (ii) 18 cm², (iii) 30 cm².
  • Q: 2. Find the area of each of the following trapezium. (i) Parallel sides 0.6 m and 1.8 m, altitude 0.5 m. (ii) Parallel sides 30 mm and 50 mm, altitude 20 mm. (iii) Parallel sides 15 cm and 20 cm, altitude 8 cm.
    Ans: Formula: Area of trapezium = 1/2 × altitude × (sum of parallel sides)
    (i) A = 1/2 × 0.5 × (0.6 + 1.8) = 1/2 × 0.5 × 2.4 = 0.6 m²
    (ii) A = 1/2 × 20 × (30 + 50) = 1/2 × 20 × 80 = 800 mm²
    (iii) A = 1/2 × 8 × (15 + 20) = 1/2 × 8 × 35 = 140 cm²
    Answer: (i) 0.6 m², (ii) 800 mm², (iii) 140 cm².
  • Q: 3. Find the area of a parallelogram, when: (i) Length of base = 6 cm, and altitude = 4 cm. (ii) Length of base = 3.8 cm and altitude = 2.2 cm.
    Ans: Formula: Area of parallelogram = base × altitude
    (i) A = 6 × 4 = 24 cm²
    (ii) A = 3.8 × 2.2 = 8.36 cm²
    Answer: (i) 24 cm², (ii) 8.36 cm².
  • Q: 4. Find the area of a triangle whose: (i) Base = 8 cm and altitude = 5 cm (ii) Base = 7.5 cm and altitude = 4 cm
    Ans: Formula: Area of triangle = 1/2 × base × altitude
    (i) A = 1/2 × 8 × 5 = 20 cm²
    (ii) A = 1/2 × 7.5 × 4 = 15 cm²
    Answer: (i) 20 cm², (ii) 15 cm².
  • Q: 5. Find the area of a trapezium when: (i) Length of base 1 = 6 cm, Length of base 2 = 4 cm, and altitude = 3 cm. (ii) Length of base 1 = 9.2 cm, length of base 2 = 6.8 cm, and altitude = 4 cm
    Ans: Formula: Area of trapezium = 1/2 × altitude × (base 1 + base 2)
    (i) A = 1/2 × 3 × (6 + 4) = 1/2 × 3 × 10 = 15 cm²
    (ii) A = 1/2 × 4 × (9.2 + 6.8) = 1/2 × 4 × 16 = 32 cm²
    Answer: (i) 15 cm², (ii) 32 cm².
  • Q: 6. Aslam prepared parallelogram piece of land having base 18 m and altitude 8 m. Find the expenditure on planting grass when the rate of plantation is 0.35 rupees per square meter.
    Ans: Formula: Area of parallelogram = base × altitude
    Area of the land = 18 × 8 = 144 m²
    Expenditure = 144 × 0.35 = 50.4
    Answer: The expenditure on planting grass is Rs. 50.40.
  • Q: 7. Base and altitude of a triangular farm are 570 m and 295 m respectively. If the rate of wheat production per square meter is 6 kg, find the total yield of wheat the farm would give.
    Ans: Formula: Area of triangle = 1/2 × base × altitude
    Area of the farm = 1/2 × 570 × 295 = 285 × 295 = 84075 m²
    Total yield = 84075 × 6 = 504450 kg
    Answer: The total yield of wheat is 504,450 kg.
  • Q: 8. The diagram shows a piece of metal which is to be used for making a saw blade. The piece is a trapezium: its two parallel sides are 16 cm and 8 cm, and the distance between them (the length of the piece) is 75 cm. Find its area.
    Ans: Formula: Area of trapezium = 1/2 × distance between parallel sides × (sum of parallel sides)
    A = 1/2 × 75 × (16 + 8)
    A = 1/2 × 75 × 24
    A = 75 × 12 = 900 cm²
    Answer: The area of the piece of metal is 900 cm².

mcqs.q: Find the area of a triangle with base 10 cm and altitude 4 cm.
mcqs.why: Area of triangle = one-half x base x altitude. Step 1: Substitute base = 10 cm and altitude = 4 cm: A = one-half x 10 x 4. Step 2: 10 x 4 = 40. Step 3: One-half of 40 = 20. So the area is 20 square cm.

mcqs.q: Find the area of a trapezium with parallel sides 0.6 m and 1.8 m and altitude 0.5 m.
mcqs.why: Area of trapezium = one-half x altitude x (sum of parallel sides). Step 1: Sum of parallel sides = 0.6 + 1.8 = 2.4 m. Step 2: A = one-half x 0.5 x 2.4. Step 3: One-half x 2.4 = 1.2, and 1.2 x 0.5 = 0.6. So the area is 0.6 square metres.

mcqs.q: Find the area of a trapezium with parallel sides 30 mm and 50 mm and altitude 20 mm.
mcqs.why: Area of trapezium = one-half x altitude x (sum of parallel sides). Step 1: Sum of parallel sides = 30 + 50 = 80 mm. Step 2: A = one-half x 20 x 80. Step 3: One-half x 20 = 10, and 10 x 80 = 800. So the area is 800 square mm.

mcqs.q: Find the area of a parallelogram with base 6 cm and altitude 4 cm.
mcqs.why: Area of parallelogram = base x altitude. Step 1: Base = 6 cm and altitude = 4 cm. Step 2: A = 6 x 4 = 24. So the area of the parallelogram is 24 square cm.

mcqs.q: Find the area of a parallelogram with base 3.8 cm and altitude 2.2 cm.
mcqs.why: Area of parallelogram = base x altitude. Step 1: Base = 3.8 cm and altitude = 2.2 cm. Step 2: A = 3.8 x 2.2. Step 3: 38 x 22 = 836, so 3.8 x 2.2 = 8.36. The area is 8.36 square cm.

mcqs.q: Find the area of a triangle with base 7.5 cm and altitude 4 cm.
mcqs.why: Area of triangle = one-half x base x altitude. Step 1: Substitute base = 7.5 cm and altitude = 4 cm: A = one-half x 7.5 x 4. Step 2: 7.5 x 4 = 30. Step 3: One-half of 30 = 15. So the area is 15 square cm.

mcqs.q: Find the area of a trapezium with bases 9.2 cm and 6.8 cm and altitude 4 cm.
mcqs.why: Area of trapezium = one-half x altitude x (base 1 + base 2). Step 1: Sum of bases = 9.2 + 6.8 = 16 cm. Step 2: A = one-half x 4 x 16. Step 3: One-half x 4 = 2, and 2 x 16 = 32. So the area is 32 square cm.

mcqs.q: A parallelogram piece of land has base 18 m and altitude 8 m. Planting grass costs Rs. 0.35 per square metre. What is the total expenditure?
mcqs.why: Area of parallelogram = base x altitude. Step 1: Area of land = 18 x 8 = 144 square metres. Step 2: Expenditure = area x rate = 144 x 0.35. Step 3: 144 x 0.35 = 50.4. So the expenditure is Rs. 50.40.

mcqs.q: A triangular farm has base 570 m and altitude 295 m. Wheat yield is 6 kg per square metre. What is the total yield?
mcqs.why: Area of triangle = one-half x base x altitude. Step 1: Area = one-half x 570 x 295 = 285 x 295 = 84075 square metres. Step 2: Total yield = 84075 x 6 = 504450 kg. So the farm gives 504,450 kg of wheat.

mcqs.q: A trapezium piece of metal has parallel sides 16 cm and 8 cm, and the distance between them is 75 cm. Find its area.
mcqs.why: Area of trapezium = one-half x distance between parallel sides x (sum of parallel sides). Step 1: Sum of parallel sides = 16 + 8 = 24 cm. Step 2: A = one-half x 75 x 24. Step 3: One-half x 24 = 12, and 75 x 12 = 900. So the area is 900 square cm.

lessons.title: Review Exercise 11
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Perimeter of square = 4 × side and Area of square = side × side; side = Perimeter ÷ 4, and side = √Area.
  • Perimeter of rectangle = 2(length + width) and Area of rectangle = length × width; missing sides are found by reversing these formulas.
  • Area of parallelogram = base × altitude, so base = Area ÷ altitude.
  • Area of triangle = ½ × base × altitude; Area of trapezium = ½ × altitude × (sum of parallel sides).
  • Perimeter is measured in length units (cm, m) and area in square units (cm², m²); an equilateral triangle has Perimeter = 3 × side.

Review Exercise 11

  • MCQ: 1(i). Choose the correct answer. Perimeter of a square having one side equal to 15 cm is:
    (a) 225 cm²   (b) 60 cm   (c) 225 cm   (d) 60 cm²
    Correct answer: 60 cm
  • MCQ: 1(ii). Choose the correct answer. Perimeter of a square is 16.8 cm. Length of its side is:
    (a) 4.2 cm   (b) 0.42 cm   (c) 8.4 cm   (d) 67.2 cm
    Correct answer: 4.2 cm
  • MCQ: 1(iii). Choose the correct answer. Perimeter of a rectangle having length 11 cm and width 8 cm is:
    (a) 76 cm²   (b) 88 cm   (c) 19 cm   (d) 38 cm
    Correct answer: 38 cm
  • MCQ: 1(iv). Choose the correct answer. Perimeter of a rectangle is 208 cm. Its length is 57 cm. Its width is:
    (a) 47 cm   (b) 151 cm   (c) 94 cm   (d) 52 cm
    Correct answer: 47 cm
  • MCQ: 1(v). Choose the correct answer. Area of a square having one side 15 cm is:
    (a) 60 cm²   (b) 225 cm²   (c) 11.5 cm²   (d) 155 cm²
    Correct answer: 225 cm²
  • MCQ: 1(vi). Choose the correct answer. Area of a rectangle having length 0.9 m and width 0.5 m is:
    (a) 4.5 m²   (b) 2.8 m²   (c) 0.045 m²   (d) 0.45 m²
    Correct answer: 0.45 m²
  • MCQ: 1(vii). Choose the correct answer. Base of a parallelogram is 10 cm. What will be the area of the parallelogram if the length of its altitude is 7 cm?
    (a) 34 cm²   (b) 68 cm²   (c) 70 cm²   (d) 35 cm²
    Correct answer: 70 cm²
  • MCQ: 1(viii). Choose the correct answer. Area of a triangle having its base 9 cm and altitude 10 cm is:
    (a) 90 cm²   (b) 45 cm²   (c) 76 cm²   (d) 19 cm²
    Correct answer: 45 cm²
  • MCQ: 1(ix). Choose the correct answer. Bases of a trapezium are 9 cm and 6 cm. If its altitude is 4 cm, its area is:
    (a) 30 cm²   (b) 60 cm²   (c) 36 cm²   (d) 24 cm²
    Correct answer: 30 cm²
  • MCQ: 1(x). Choose the correct answer. Area of a parallelogram is 36 m². If the length of its altitude (printed 'attitude') is 4 m, what is its base:
    (a) 6 m   (b) 32 m²   (c) 18 m   (d) 9 m
    Correct answer: 9 m
  • Q: 2. Write an expression for the area and the perimeter of each figure. Simplify each expression. (i) A rectangle with length 5x² and width 3x². (ii) A rectangle with length 7y and width 4x. (iii) A square with side a.
    Ans: Formula: Area of rectangle = length × width; Perimeter of rectangle = 2(length + width).
    (i) Area = 5x² × 3x² = 15x⁴
    Perimeter = 2(5x² + 3x²) = 2 × 8x² = 16x²
    Answer: (i) Area = 15x⁴, Perimeter = 16x².
    (ii) Area = 7y × 4x = 28xy
    Perimeter = 2(4x + 7y) = 8x + 14y
    Answer: (ii) Area = 28xy, Perimeter = 8x + 14y.
    (iii) Formula: Area of square = side × side; Perimeter of square = 4 × side.
    Area = a × a = a²
    Perimeter = 4a
    Answer: (iii) Area = a², Perimeter = 4a.
  • Q: 3. Find the area of each figure. (i) A parallelogram with base 3 ft and the side marked 4 ft. (ii) A triangle with base 3 cm and altitude 5.4 cm. (iii) A trapezium with parallel sides 8 m and 7.6 m and altitude 6 m.
    Ans: (i) Formula: Area of parallelogram = base × altitude
    A = 3 × 4 = 12 ft²
    Answer: (i) 12 square feet.
    Note: The figure marks 4 ft on the side of the parallelogram; the book evidently intends it as the height belonging to the base of 3 ft.
    (ii) Formula: Area of triangle = 1/2 × base × altitude
    A = 1/2 × 3 × 5.4 = 8.1 cm²
    Answer: (ii) 8.1 cm².
    (iii) Formula: Area of trapezium = 1/2 × altitude × (sum of parallel sides)
    A = 1/2 × 6 × (8 + 7.6) = 1/2 × 6 × 15.6 = 46.8 m²
    Answer: (iii) 46.8 m².
  • Q: 4. Area of a right-angled triangle is 21bc square centimetre (as printed). If the area is equal to 15 sq. cm, and b = 5, then find c.
    Ans: Formula: Area of a right-angled triangle = 1/2 × base × height, i.e. Area = 1/2 bc.
    1/2 bc = 15
    1/2 × 5 × c = 15
    5c = 15 × 2 = 30
    c = 30 ÷ 5 = 6
    Answer: c = 6 cm.
    Note: The book prints '21bc', which is a misprint for '1/2 bc' — the area of a right-angled triangle with sides b and c around the right angle.
  • Q: 5. If the perimeter of an equilateral triangle is 15 cm, find the length of each side.
    Ans: An equilateral triangle has all three sides equal.
    Formula: Perimeter = 3 × length of one side
    15 = 3 × side
    Side = 15 ÷ 3 = 5
    Answer: The length of each side is 5 cm.
  • Q: 6. Perimeter of a rectangle is 125 cm. If the breadth of the rectangle is 25 cm, find its length.
    Ans: Formula: Perimeter of rectangle = 2(length + breadth)
    125 = 2(l + 25)
    l + 25 = 125 ÷ 2 = 62.5
    l = 62.5 − 25 = 37.5
    Answer: The length of the rectangle is 37.5 cm.
  • Q: 7. Perimeter of a rectangle is 50 metre. If the length of the rectangle is 15 metre, find its breadth.
    Ans: Formula: Perimeter of rectangle = 2(length + breadth)
    50 = 2(15 + b)
    15 + b = 50 ÷ 2 = 25
    b = 25 − 15 = 10
    Answer: The breadth of the rectangle is 10 m.
  • Q: 8. Area of a rectangular field is 90 square metre. If its length is 12 metre, find its breadth.
    Ans: Formula: Area of rectangle = length × breadth
    90 = 12 × b
    b = 90 ÷ 12 = 7.5
    Answer: The breadth of the field is 7.5 m.
  • Q: 9. Area of a square field is 225 sq. metre. Find the length of its sides.
    Ans: Formula: Area of square = side × side
    side × side = 225
    side = √225 = 15, because 15 × 15 = 225
    Answer: The length of each side is 15 m.
  • Q: 10. Perimeter of a square is 14 cm. Find length of its side.
    Ans: Formula: Perimeter of square = 4 × side
    14 = 4 × side
    Side = 14 ÷ 4 = 3.5
    Answer: The length of its side is 3.5 cm.

mcqs.q: Perimeter of a square having one side equal to 15 cm is:
mcqs.why: Perimeter of square = 4 x side. Step 1: Side = 15 cm. Step 2: P = 4 x 15 = 60 cm. Perimeter is a length, so the unit is cm, not square cm.

mcqs.q: Perimeter of a square is 16.8 cm. Length of its side is:
mcqs.why: Perimeter of square = 4 x side, so side = Perimeter divided by 4. Step 1: Perimeter = 16.8 cm. Step 2: Side = 16.8 divided by 4 = 4.2 cm.

mcqs.q: Perimeter of a rectangle having length 11 cm and width 8 cm is:
mcqs.why: Perimeter of rectangle = 2(length + width). Step 1: Length + width = 11 + 8 = 19 cm. Step 2: P = 2 x 19 = 38 cm. Perimeter is a length, so the unit is cm.

mcqs.q: Perimeter of a rectangle is 208 cm. Its length is 57 cm. Its width is:
mcqs.why: Perimeter of rectangle = 2(length + width). Step 1: 208 = 2(57 + w), so 57 + w = 208 divided by 2 = 104. Step 2: w = 104 - 57 = 47. So the width is 47 cm.

mcqs.q: Area of a square having one side 15 cm is:
mcqs.why: Area of square = side x side. Step 1: Side = 15 cm. Step 2: A = 15 x 15 = 225. So the area is 225 square cm.

mcqs.q: Area of a rectangle having length 0.9 m and width 0.5 m is:
mcqs.why: Area of rectangle = length x width. Step 1: Length = 0.9 m and width = 0.5 m. Step 2: A = 0.9 x 0.5 = 0.45. So the area is 0.45 square metres.

mcqs.q: Base of a parallelogram is 10 cm. What will be the area of the parallelogram if the length of its altitude is 7 cm?
mcqs.why: Area of parallelogram = base x altitude. Step 1: Base = 10 cm and altitude = 7 cm. Step 2: A = 10 x 7 = 70. So the area is 70 square cm.

mcqs.q: Area of a triangle having its base 9 cm and altitude 10 cm is:
mcqs.why: Area of triangle = one-half x base x altitude. Step 1: A = one-half x 9 x 10. Step 2: 9 x 10 = 90. Step 3: One-half of 90 = 45. So the area is 45 square cm.

mcqs.q: Bases of a trapezium are 9 cm and 6 cm. If its altitude is 4 cm, its area is:
mcqs.why: Area of trapezium = one-half x altitude x (sum of parallel sides). Step 1: Sum of bases = 9 + 6 = 15 cm. Step 2: A = one-half x 4 x 15. Step 3: One-half x 4 = 2, and 2 x 15 = 30. So the area is 30 square cm.

mcqs.q: Area of a parallelogram is 36 m². If the length of its altitude is 4 m, what is its base?
mcqs.why: Area of parallelogram = base x altitude, so base = Area divided by altitude. Step 1: Area = 36 square metres and altitude = 4 m. Step 2: Base = 36 divided by 4 = 9 m. The book prints altitude as attitude, which is a spelling misprint. Base is a length, so the unit is m.

mcqs.q: A rectangle has length 5x² and width 3x². What is its area?
mcqs.why: Area of rectangle = length x width. Step 1: Area = 5x squared x 3x squared. Step 2: Multiply numbers: 5 x 3 = 15. Step 3: Multiply powers: x squared x x squared = x to the power 4. So the area is 15x to the power 4. For reference, Perimeter of rectangle = 2(length + width) = 16x squared.

mcqs.q: A trapezium has parallel sides 8 m and 7.6 m and altitude 6 m. Find its area.
mcqs.why: Area of trapezium = one-half x altitude x (sum of parallel sides). Step 1: Sum of parallel sides = 8 + 7.6 = 15.6 m. Step 2: A = one-half x 6 x 15.6. Step 3: One-half x 6 = 3, and 3 x 15.6 = 46.8. So the area is 46.8 square metres.

mcqs.q: The area of a right-angled triangle with sides b and c around the right angle is 15 sq. cm, and b = 5. Find c.
mcqs.why: Area of a right-angled triangle = one-half x base x height, here Area = one-half bc. Step 1: One-half x 5 x c = 15. Step 2: 5c = 15 x 2 = 30. Step 3: c = 30 divided by 5 = 6 cm. The book prints 21bc, which is a misprint for one-half bc.

mcqs.q: The perimeter of an equilateral triangle is 15 cm. Find the length of each side.
mcqs.why: An equilateral triangle has all three sides equal, so Perimeter = 3 x length of one side. Step 1: 15 = 3 x side. Step 2: Side = 15 divided by 3 = 5. So each side is 5 cm long.

mcqs.q: The perimeter of a rectangle is 125 cm and its breadth is 25 cm. Find its length.
mcqs.why: Perimeter of rectangle = 2(length + breadth). Step 1: 125 = 2(l + 25), so l + 25 = 125 divided by 2 = 62.5. Step 2: l = 62.5 - 25 = 37.5. So the length is 37.5 cm.

lessons.title: Exercise 12
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Surface area of a cube = 6a^2, where a is the length of one side.
  • Surface area of a cuboid = 2(lb + bh + hl).
  • Volume of a cube = a^3; volume of a cuboid = length x breadth x height.
  • An open cubical pool has only 5 faces, so its surface area is 5 times the area of one face.
  • Depth of a box = Volume / base area; a sphere has no edges and no vertices, a cylinder has 2 edges, and a cone has one vertex.

Exercise 12

  • Q: 1. Find the surface area of a cube whose one side is: (i) 5 cm (ii) 4.5 cm (iii) 7.8 cm (iv) 6.9 cm
    Ans: Formula: Surface area of a cube = 6a², where a is the length of one side.
    (i) Surface area = 6 × 5² = 6 × 25 = 150 cm²
    (ii) Surface area = 6 × 4.5² = 6 × 20.25 = 121.5 cm²
    (iii) Surface area = 6 × 7.8² = 6 × 60.84 = 365.04 cm²
    (iv) Surface area = 6 × 6.9² = 6 × 47.61 = 285.66 cm²
    Answer: (i) 150 cm², (ii) 121.5 cm², (iii) 365.04 cm², (iv) 285.66 cm².
  • Q: 2. Find the surface areas of the following cuboids. (i) Length 4 cm, Breadth 3 cm, Height 2 cm. (ii) Length 5 cm, Breadth 4 cm, Height 9 cm. (iii) Length 7.5 m, Breadth 3.4 m, Height 2 m.
    Ans: Formula: Surface area of a cuboid = 2(lb + bh + hl)
    (i) = 2(4 × 3 + 3 × 2 + 2 × 4) = 2(12 + 6 + 8) = 2 × 26 = 52 cm²
    (ii) = 2(5 × 4 + 4 × 9 + 9 × 5) = 2(20 + 36 + 45) = 2 × 101 = 202 cm²
    (iii) = 2(7.5 × 3.4 + 3.4 × 2 + 2 × 7.5) = 2(25.5 + 6.8 + 15) = 2 × 47.3 = 94.6 m²
    Answer: (i) 52 cm², (ii) 202 cm², (iii) 94.6 m².
  • Q: 3. Find volume of the cube whose one side is (i) 1 cm (ii) 6 cm (iii) 4.5 m (iv) 5.4 m
    Ans: Formula: Volume of a cube = a³, where a is the length of one side.
    (i) Volume = 1³ = 1 × 1 × 1 = 1 cm³
    (ii) Volume = 6³ = 6 × 6 × 6 = 216 cm³
    (iii) Volume = 4.5³ = 4.5 × 4.5 × 4.5 = 91.125 m³
    (iv) Volume = 5.4³ = 5.4 × 5.4 × 5.4 = 157.464 m³
    Answer: (i) 1 cm³, (ii) 216 cm³, (iii) 91.125 m³, (iv) 157.464 m³.
  • Q: 4. Find volume of the cuboids whose length, breadth, and height are given in question 2 above. (i) 4 cm, 3 cm, 2 cm. (ii) 5 cm, 4 cm, 9 cm. (iii) 7.5 m, 3.4 m, 2 m.
    Ans: Formula: Volume of a cuboid = length × breadth × height
    (i) Volume = 4 × 3 × 2 = 24 cm³
    (ii) Volume = 5 × 4 × 9 = 180 cm³
    (iii) Volume = 7.5 × 3.4 × 2 = 51 m³
    Answer: (i) 24 cm³, (ii) 180 cm³, (iii) 51 m³.
  • Q: 5. The side of a cubical pool is 5 meters. Find its (i) Surface area (ii) Volume. Note (as printed in the book): Since the pool is open, its surface area will be sum of surface areas of 5 faces.
    Ans: (i) The pool is open at the top, so it has only 5 faces (as stated in the book's Note).
    Area of one face = 5 × 5 = 25 m²
    Surface area = 5 × 25 = 125 m²
    Answer: (i) Surface area = 125 m².
    (ii) Formula: Volume of a cube = a³
    Volume = 5 × 5 × 5 = 125 m³
    Answer: (ii) Volume = 125 m³.
  • Q: 6. A rectangular room is 4.5 m long, 3.5 m wide and 5 m deep. Find its (i) Surface area (ii) Volume
    Ans: Formula: Surface area of a cuboid = 2(lb + bh + hl)
    (i) Surface area = 2(4.5 × 3.5 + 3.5 × 5 + 5 × 4.5)
    = 2(15.75 + 17.5 + 22.5)
    = 2 × 55.75 = 111.5 m²
    Answer: (i) Surface area = 111.5 m².
    Formula: Volume of a cuboid = length × breadth × height
    (ii) Volume = 4.5 × 3.5 × 5 = 78.75 m³
    Answer: (ii) Volume = 78.75 m³.
  • Q: 7. Volume of a box is 60 cm³. If its base area is 20 cm². Find its depth.
    Ans: Formula: Volume = base area × depth, so depth = Volume ÷ base area
    Depth = 60 ÷ 20 = 3
    Answer: The depth of the box is 3 cm.
  • Q: 8. Give 2 examples of a sphere and draw their figures.
    Ans: Two examples of a sphere are: (1) a football, (2) a cricket ball. (The book also names the hockey ball.)
    How to draw the figure: Draw a circle. Mark its centre C and draw a radius line from C to a point A on the circle. This round figure represents a sphere, which has no edges and no vertices; its curved outer part is its surface.
  • Q: 9. Give 2 examples of a cylinder and draw their figures
    Ans: Two examples of a cylinder are: (1) a tin of ghee, (2) a jar. (The book also names a pencil.)
    How to draw the figure: Draw two equal circles, one at the top and one at the bottom, and join them with a curved surface. A cylinder has 2 edges, 2 plane circular faces and one curved surface.
  • Q: 10. Give 2 examples of a cone and draw their figures.
    Ans: Two examples of a cone are: (1) an ice-cream cone, (2) a conical birthday cap.
    How to draw the figure: Draw a circle as the base (plane surface) and join its edge by a slanting (curved) surface to a single point at the top, called the vertex. A cone has one circular face, one edge and one vertex.

mcqs.q: Find the surface area of a cube whose one side is 5 cm.
mcqs.why: Formula: Surface area of a cube = 6a^2, where a is the side. Step 1: a = 5, so a^2 = 5 x 5 = 25. Step 2: Multiply by 6: 6 x 25 = 150. Surface area = 150 cm^2.

mcqs.q: Find the surface area of a cube whose one side is 7.8 cm.
mcqs.why: Formula: Surface area of a cube = 6a^2. Step 1: a = 7.8, so a^2 = 7.8 x 7.8 = 60.84. Step 2: Multiply by 6: 6 x 60.84 = 365.04. Surface area = 365.04 cm^2.

mcqs.q: Find the surface area of a cuboid with length 4 cm, breadth 3 cm and height 2 cm.
mcqs.why: Formula: Surface area of a cuboid = 2(lb + bh + hl). Step 1: lb = 4 x 3 = 12, bh = 3 x 2 = 6, hl = 2 x 4 = 8. Step 2: Add: 12 + 6 + 8 = 26. Step 3: Multiply by 2: 2 x 26 = 52 cm^2.

mcqs.q: Find the surface area of a cuboid with length 5 cm, breadth 4 cm and height 9 cm.
mcqs.why: Formula: Surface area of a cuboid = 2(lb + bh + hl). Step 1: lb = 5 x 4 = 20, bh = 4 x 9 = 36, hl = 9 x 5 = 45. Step 2: Add: 20 + 36 + 45 = 101. Step 3: Multiply by 2: 2 x 101 = 202 cm^2.

mcqs.q: Find the volume of a cube whose one side is 6 cm.
mcqs.why: Formula: Volume of a cube = a^3. Step 1: a = 6. Step 2: Multiply step by step: 6 x 6 = 36, then 36 x 6 = 216. Volume = 216 cm^3.

mcqs.q: Find the volume of a cube whose one side is 4.5 m.
mcqs.why: Formula: Volume of a cube = a^3. Step 1: a = 4.5. Step 2: Multiply: 4.5 x 4.5 = 20.25. Step 3: Multiply again: 20.25 x 4.5 = 91.125. Volume = 91.125 m^3.

mcqs.q: Find the volume of a cuboid with length 5 cm, breadth 4 cm and height 9 cm.
mcqs.why: Formula: Volume of a cuboid = length x breadth x height. Step 1: Multiply length and breadth: 5 x 4 = 20. Step 2: Multiply by height: 20 x 9 = 180. Volume = 180 cm^3.

mcqs.q: A cubical pool is open at the top and its side is 5 m. Find its surface area.
mcqs.why: The pool is open, so only 5 faces are counted, as stated in the book. Step 1: Area of one face = 5 x 5 = 25 m^2. Step 2: Multiply by the 5 faces: 5 x 25 = 125. Surface area = 125 m^2.

mcqs.q: The volume of a box is 60 cm^3 and its base area is 20 cm^2. Find its depth.
mcqs.why: Formula: Volume = base area x depth, so depth = Volume / base area. Step 1: Write the values: Volume = 60, base area = 20. Step 2: Divide: 60 / 20 = 3. Depth = 3 cm.

mcqs.q: How many edges does a cylinder have?
mcqs.why: A cylinder has 2 plane circular faces, one at the top and one at the bottom, and one curved surface joining them. The boundary of each circular face is an edge, so a cylinder has 2 edges.

lessons.title: Review Exercise 12
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Figures that lie in a plane, such as a triangle and a square, are two dimensional; a cuboid is a three dimensional figure.
  • Surface area of a cube of side a = 6a^2; volume of a cube of side a = a^3.
  • Surface area of a cuboid of sides a, b, c = 2ab + 2bc + 2ca.
  • Volume of a cuboid = length x breadth x height, for example 3 x 2 x 1 = 6 cm^3.
  • The volume of a cube of side 1 m is 1 x 1 x 1 = 1 m^3.

Review Exercise 12

  • Fill in the blank: 1. A triangle lies in two dimension.
  • Fill in the blank: 2. Figures which lie in plane are called two dimensional.
  • Fill in the blank: 3. □ (a square) is a two dimensional figure.
  • Fill in the blank: 4. A cuboid is a three (3) D-figure.
  • Fill in the blank: 5. Surface area of cube of a cm side = 6a² cm².
  • Fill in the blank: 6. Volume of a cube of a cm side = a³ cm³.
  • Fill in the blank: 7. Surface area of cuboid of sides a cm, b cm and c cm = 2ab + 2bc + 2ca cm².
  • Fill in the blank: 8. Volume of cube of side 1 m = 1 m³.
  • Fill in the blank: 9. Volume of cuboid of sides 3 cm, 2 cm, 1 cm = 6 cm³.
  • Q: 10. Which figure does not have the same dimensions as the other figures? The four figures are cuboids labelled A, B, C and D, drawn in different positions with no measurements marked.
    Ans: A, B and C are the same cuboid drawn in different positions: each has one long edge, one medium edge and one short edge — A shows it lying with the long face in front, B shows the same box standing upright, and C shows it lying flat.
    Figure D is different: its front face is nearly square and all its edges are comparatively closer in length, so its three dimensions are not the same set as those of A, B and C.
    Answer: Figure D does not have the same dimensions as the other figures.
    Note: The figures carry no printed measurements; the answer is found by comparing the lengths of the three edges of each cuboid as drawn.

mcqs.q: A triangle lies in how many dimensions?
mcqs.why: A triangle is a flat figure that lies in a plane. Figures that lie in a plane have length and breadth only, so a triangle lies in two dimensions.

mcqs.q: Figures which lie in a plane are called:
mcqs.why: Figures which lie in a plane have only length and breadth and no thickness. Such figures are called two dimensional figures.

mcqs.q: A square is which type of figure?
mcqs.why: A square lies flat in a plane and has only length and breadth. Therefore a square is a two dimensional figure.

mcqs.q: A cuboid is a:
mcqs.why: A cuboid has length, breadth and height, so it occupies space in three directions. Therefore a cuboid is a three (3) D-figure.

mcqs.q: The surface area of a cube of side a cm is:
mcqs.why: Formula: Surface area of a cube = 6a^2. A cube has 6 equal square faces, and the area of one face is a x a = a^2, so the total surface area is 6 x a^2 = 6a^2 cm^2.

mcqs.q: The volume of a cube of side a cm is:
mcqs.why: Formula: Volume of a cube = a^3. Volume is found by multiplying the side three times: a x a x a = a^3, so the volume of a cube of side a cm is a^3 cm^3.

mcqs.q: The surface area of a cuboid of sides a cm, b cm and c cm is:
mcqs.why: Formula: Surface area of a cuboid = 2(lb + bh + hl). With sides a, b and c this becomes 2(ab + bc + ca), which expanded is 2ab + 2bc + 2ca cm^2.

mcqs.q: What is the volume of a cube of side 1 m?
mcqs.why: Formula: Volume of a cube = a^3. Step 1: a = 1 m. Step 2: Multiply step by step: 1 x 1 = 1, then 1 x 1 = 1. Volume = 1 m^3.

mcqs.q: What is the volume of a cuboid of sides 3 cm, 2 cm and 1 cm?
mcqs.why: Formula: Volume of a cuboid = length x breadth x height. Step 1: Multiply the first two sides: 3 x 2 = 6. Step 2: Multiply by the third side: 6 x 1 = 6. Volume = 6 cm^3.

mcqs.q: Four cuboids A, B, C and D are drawn in different positions. A, B and C are the same cuboid in different positions, while D has a nearly square front face with edges closer in length. Which figure does not have the same dimensions as the others?
mcqs.why: A, B and C each have one long edge, one medium edge and one short edge, so they are the same cuboid drawn in different positions. Figure D has different edge lengths, with a nearly square front face, so Figure D does not have the same dimensions.

lessons.title: Exercises 13.1, 13.2 and 13.3
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Grouped data is raw data arranged in different groups; ungrouped data is numerical facts given as obtained, not arranged in groups.
  • In a bar graph the bars have equal width with equal spaces between them, and a suitable scale is chosen, such as 1 big square = 50 km or 1 big square = 5 mm.
  • In a pie graph the bigger the angle of a sector, the greater the value it represents, and all sector angles add up to 360 degrees.
  • Fraction from a percentage: fraction = percentage / 100, then simplify, for example 25% = 25/100 = 1/4.
  • Number of people for a sector = percentage / 100 x total, for example Drive = 40/100 x 400 = 160 people.

Exercise 13.1

  • Q: 1. Define grouped data and give one example.
    Ans: Grouped data: Raw data when put in some order or arranged in different groups is called grouped data.
    Example (from this book): 50 students of class 6th are divided into 5 groups according to their scores out of 100 in Mathematics — Scores 0–20: 5 students, 20–40: 10 students, 40–60: 15 students, 60–80: 5 students, 80–100: 15 students. This is grouped data because the marks are arranged in groups.
  • Q: 2. Define ungrouped data and give one example.
    Ans: Ungrouped data: Numerical facts which are obtained as such (in their original form, not arranged in groups) are known as ungrouped data.
    Example (from this book): 5 students of class 6th obtained 95, 94, 93, 92 and 91 marks out of 100 in Mathematics. These marks are given just as obtained, so this is ungrouped data.
  • Q: 3. The number of patients of kidney problems admitted in hospital during a week according to their ages given below. 40, 36, 17, 25, 12, 13, 31, 36, 47, 32, 26, 10, 15, 6, 45, 20, 9, 60, 19, 4, 14. Identify the type of this data.
    Ans: Method: Data given as a plain list of separate values, not arranged in groups or classes, is ungrouped data.
    The ages are listed one by one as obtained: 40, 36, 17, 25, 12, 13, 31, 36, 47, 32, 26, 10, 15, 6, 45, 20, 9, 60, 19, 4, 14. They are not put into any groups.
    Answer: This is ungrouped data.
  • Q: 4. Given below are the marks out of 50 obtained by 40 students of class 6 in a test of mathematics. Marks obtained: 15–20: 10 students; 21–26: 7 students; 27–32: 6 students; 33–38: 8 students; 39–44: 6 students; 45–50: 3 students; Total: 40 students. Qasim Shah thinks it as a grouped data while Yasmin thinks it as an ungrouped data. Who is correct?
    Ans: Method: When raw data is arranged in different groups (classes) with the number of observations in each group, it is grouped data.
    In the table the marks are arranged in the groups 15–20, 21–26, 27–32, 33–38, 39–44 and 45–50, with the number of students in each group. So the data is grouped data.
    Answer: Qasim Shah is correct; Yasmin is not correct.

Exercise 13.2

  • Q: 1. Draw a vertical bar graph to represent speed of a car in first four hours given below. Time: 1st hour, 2nd hour, 3rd hour, 4th hour. Speed: 50 km, 100 km, 150 km, 200 km.
    Ans: Data: 1st hour: 50 km; 2nd hour: 100 km; 3rd hour: 150 km; 4th hour: 200 km.
    Method: For a vertical bar graph, draw two mutually perpendicular rays OX (horizontal) and OY (vertical) meeting at O.
    Step 1: Show the hours (1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th) along OX at equal gaps.
    Step 2: Choose the scale along OY: 1 big square = 50 km.
    Step 3: Draw bars of equal width with equal spaces between them, with heights: 1st hour = 50 (up to 50), 2nd hour = 100 (up to 100), 3rd hour = 150 (up to 150), 4th hour = 200 (up to 200).
    The four rising bars, reaching 50, 100, 150 and 200 on the speed axis, form the required vertical bar graph.
  • Q: 2. The amount of rainfall in Peshawar recorded from April to September is given below. Draw vertical bar graph. Months: April, May, June, July, August, September. Rain fall in mm: 15, 18, 20, 25, 28, 30.
    Ans: Data: April: 15 mm; May: 18 mm; June: 20 mm; July: 25 mm; August: 28 mm; September: 30 mm.
    Method: For a vertical bar graph, draw two mutually perpendicular rays OX (horizontal) and OY (vertical) meeting at O.
    Step 1: Show the months (April, May, June, July, August, September) along OX at equal gaps.
    Step 2: Choose the scale along OY: 1 big square = 5 mm of rainfall, marking 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30.
    Step 3: Draw bars of equal width with equal spaces between them, with heights: April = 15, May = 18, June = 20, July = 25, August = 28, September = 30.
    The six bars, reaching 15, 18, 20, 25, 28 and 30 on the rainfall axis, form the required vertical bar graph.
  • Q: 3. Draw a horizontal bar graph to represent the product of wheat in Charsadda during the year 1990 to 1994. Years: 1990, 1991, 1992, 1993, 1994. Production in tons: 90, 100, 115, 120, 110.
    Ans: Data: 1990: 90 tons; 1991: 100 tons; 1992: 115 tons; 1993: 120 tons; 1994: 110 tons.
    Method: For a horizontal bar graph, draw two mutually perpendicular rays OX (horizontal) and OY (vertical) meeting at O. The scale is taken along OX.
    Step 1: Show the years (1990, 1991, 1992, 1993, 1994) along OY at equal gaps.
    Step 2: Choose the scale along OX: 1 big square = 10 tons, marking 0, 10, 20, ... up to 120.
    Step 3: Draw horizontal bars of equal width with equal spaces between them, with lengths: 1990 = 90, 1991 = 100, 1992 = 115, 1993 = 120, 1994 = 110.
    The five horizontal bars, reaching 90, 100, 115, 120 and 110 on the production axis, form the required horizontal bar graph.
  • Q: 4. Draw a horizontal bar graph to represent monthly income of Aslam, Akram, Bilal, Ahmed and Hamza given below. Person: Aslam, Akram, Bilal, Ahmad, Hamza. Income (in Rupees): 2000, 3000, 4000, 5000, 6000.
    Ans: Data: Aslam: Rs. 2000; Akram: Rs. 3000; Bilal: Rs. 4000; Ahmad: Rs. 5000; Hamza: Rs. 6000.
    Method: For a horizontal bar graph, draw two mutually perpendicular rays OX (horizontal) and OY (vertical) meeting at O. The scale is taken along OX.
    Step 1: Show the persons (Aslam, Akram, Bilal, Ahmad, Hamza) along OY at equal gaps.
    Step 2: Choose the scale along OX: 1 big square = Rs. 1000, marking 0, 1000, 2000, ... up to 6000.
    Step 3: Draw horizontal bars of equal width with equal spaces between them, with lengths: Aslam = 2000, Akram = 3000, Bilal = 4000, Ahmad = 5000, Hamza = 6000.
    The five horizontal bars, reaching 2000, 3000, 4000, 5000 and 6000 on the income axis, form the required horizontal bar graph.

Pie Graph Questions (Section 13.3)

  • Q: 1. Use the pie chart 'A student's typical day' to answer these questions. The sectors of the pie chart are: Sleep 7 h, Work 8 h, TV 2 h, Hobbies 3.5 h, Meals 2 h, Other 1.5 h. a) Which activity took the most time? b) How much longer did the student spend on hobbies than on watching TV? c) What is the total time shown on the pie chart? Why?
    Ans: The pie chart 'A student's typical day' has 6 sectors: Sleep 7 h, Work 8 h, TV 2 h, Hobbies 3.5 h, Meals 2 h, Other 1.5 h.
    a) The biggest sector is Work, 8 h.
    Answer: a) Work took the most time (8 hours).
    b) Method: Subtract the smaller time from the bigger time.
    Hobbies − TV = 3.5 − 2 = 1.5 h
    Answer: b) The student spent 1.5 hours longer on hobbies than on watching TV.
    c) Method: Add the times of all the sectors.
    Total = 7 + 8 + 2 + 3.5 + 2 + 1.5 = 24 h
    Answer: c) The total time shown is 24 hours, because the pie chart shows the activities of one full day, and one day has 24 hours.
  • Q: 2. This pie chart shows the results of a survey about how people travel to work. The sectors are: Drive 40%, Bus 25%, Train 20%, Walk 10%, Cycle 5%. a) Which is i) the most popular way of getting to work ii) the least popular way of getting to work? b) What fraction of the people i) travel to work by bus ii) walk to work? c) Altogether 400 people took part in the survey. Find how many travelled by each method.
    Ans: The pie chart 'Travelling to work' shows: Drive 40%, Bus 25%, Train 20%, Walk 10%, Cycle 5%.
    a) Method: The biggest percentage is the most popular way and the smallest percentage is the least popular way.
    (i) The biggest sector is Drive, 40%.
    Answer: (i) The most popular way of getting to work is Drive (by car).
    (ii) The smallest sector is Cycle, 5%.
    Answer: (ii) The least popular way of getting to work is Cycle.
    b) Method: Fraction = percentage ÷ 100, then simplify.
    (i) Bus = 25/100 = 1/4
    Answer: (i) 1/4 of the people travel to work by bus.
    (ii) Walk = 10/100 = 1/10
    Answer: (ii) 1/10 of the people walk to work.
    c) Method: Number of people = percentage ÷ 100 × total people (400).
    Drive = 40/100 × 400 = 160
    Bus = 25/100 × 400 = 100
    Train = 20/100 × 400 = 80
    Walk = 10/100 × 400 = 40
    Cycle = 5/100 × 400 = 20
    Check: 160 + 100 + 80 + 40 + 20 = 400.
    Answer: c) Drive: 160 people, Bus: 100 people, Train: 80 people, Walk: 40 people, Cycle: 20 people.

Exercise 13.3

  • Q: 1. Ahmad has three types of animals as shown in pie graph, read the graph and answer the following questions. The sectors of the pie graph are: Goats 180°, Cows 120°, Chickens 60°. (i) Which type of animal is greatest in number? (ii) Which type of animal is smallest in number? (iii) Without calculation, find the ratio of goats and cows.
